data.title: Slowdown calls deflate AI stocks
data.description:
INTELLIGENT THREATS?: Several industry leaders called for a more measured and careful development of AI models over widespread concerns of misuse and harm

Stocks related to artificial intelligence (AI) fell sharply yesterday after the CEOs of the US companies developing the most advanced AI models warned the pace of development must slow to prevent threats to humanity.

Anthropic PBC CEO Dario Amodei, in a lengthy essay shared on social media on Saturday, called on AI companies to slow the rate at which they advance model capabilities amid mounting fears of AI misuse. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who runs xAI, said that they agree with Amodei.

In Japan, shares in ChatGPT maker OpenAI’s investor Softbank Group Corp tumbled as much as 13.2 percent, and memory maker Kioxia Holdings Corp plunged 9.8 percent initially, while chip supply chain company Tokyo Electron Ltd fell 3.7 percent.

In Taipei, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) slipped 1.2 percent, while in South Korea SK Hynix Inc slid 5.3 percent and Samsung Electronics Co fell 3.7 percent.

“Selling pressure is likely to hit AI and semiconductor-related stocks in Tokyo following a series of weekend comments calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development,” Sony Financial Group Inc senior economist Takayuki Miyajima said in a note. “Additionally, uncertainty surrounding the situation in the Middle East continues to weigh on sentiment.”

In Shanghai, memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies Inc (長鑫存儲) dropped as much as 3.6 percent, while Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (中芯) fell 2.6 percent.

In Hong Kong, Zhongji Innolight Co (中際旭創) shed as much as 6.7 percent at one point, while MiniMax Group Inc (稀宇科技) dropped as much as 7.8 percent. Shares of Z.AI Co (智譜), the developer of the GLM AI series, tumbled as much as 10.5 percent after making a discounted share placement.

San Francisco-based Anthropic released a threat intelligence report on Thursday detailing how several actors had used its Claude AI models for activities ranging from weapons development and cyber operations to surveillance and fraud.

Alarm about the harm from AI grew when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, saying that the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

While several US lawmakers have raised concern about AI’s rapid progress and called for new rules, US President Donald Trump on Sunday likened AI critics to “very negative forces” bringing up scenarios that would not happen, and said he wanted to make sure that the US remains the industry leader.

China’s state-backed Global Times called the Anthropic essay a “Cold War playbook” in an editorial, one intended to curb the country’s technological development.

Some investors dismissed the warnings from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Michael Burry, whose prescient bets against the US housing market before the 2008 financial crisis were chronicled in the movie The Big Short, said in a message on social media the warnings were “hype and puffery” and “cover for real uncontrollable slowing growth.”

Others said the warnings would be an overhang.

“In the short term, these warnings could still weigh on AI and chip stocks,” Saxo Bank A/S chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said. “Their valuations assume both strong demand and a relentless pace of technological progress,” she said. “When expectations are this high, even a possible delay can trigger profit-taking.”

The bigger question for markets around AI was who would ultimately earn the return on all the capital being spent on building new capacity, T Rowe Price Group Inc portfolio manager Sebastien Mallet said.

“There is little doubt that AI will change the world,” he said. “But that does not necessarily mean every investment being made today will generate an attractive return.”

data.title: Cathay raises GDP growth forecast to 11.6%
data.description:
OPTIMISTIC OUTLOOK: Growth may slow down next year, but the financial company thinks that this year’s economic growth will surpass 10 percent through the AI boom

Cathay Financial Holding Co (國泰金控) yesterday raised its forecast for Taiwan’s economic growth this year to 11.6 percent from 10.1 percent, citing stronger-than-expected artificial intelligence (AI) demand, robust exports and continued investment in AI infrastructure.

The upgrade highlights the strength of Taiwan’s AI-driven expansion, with technology exports and investment continuing to outperform expectations and offsetting weakness in other parts of the economy.

The research team, led by National Central University economics professor Hsu Chih-chiang (徐之強), forecast 5.1 percent growth for next year, as this year’s unusually strong expansion creates a high comparison base.

Hsu, co-director of the research program, said the growing adoption of AI by businesses should give US cloud service providers more room to increase capital spending, supporting Taiwan’s exports and investment in the second half of the year.

Taiwan’s exports reached a record US$82.4 billion last month, driven by strong demand for AI-related hardware and high-performance computing products.

The team expects the economy to grow about 9 percent in the second half, slightly above the 8 percent forecast by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics. The economy expanded 14 percent in the first six months, while third-quarter growth is expected to remain in double digits, it said.

While the economic growth is likely to moderate next year, AI demand is expected to remain an important source of support, Hsu said.

The team forecast consumer inflation would grow 2.1 percent this year, broadly in line with the government’s 2.07 percent projection, before easing to 1.9 percent next year.

The central bank is expected to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at its board meeting on Thursday, despite inflation remaining above its 2 percent warning threshold for the past four straight months, Hsu said.

The central bank is likely to monitor price pressures and US Federal Reserve policy before considering any tightening later this year, he said.

The team expects the central bank to refrain from tightening housing credit controls, as transactions have slowed and prices have largely stagnated.

Hsu said rising US Treasury yields could make bonds more attractive relative to equities, putting additional pressure on stocks, particularly technology shares.

A more serious risk would be an inversion of the US yield curve, he said, as it could signal deeper concerns about the economic outlook.

data.title: Automakers sign US$147m in deals at German show
data.description:
Taiwanese auto parts and accessory makers signed US$147 million in business deals while participating in Automechanika Frankfurt held over the weekend, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.

About 324 Taiwanese auto parts and accessory suppliers, including manufacturers of car door handles, bumpers, metal components and automotive electronics, took part in the Frankfurt trade exhibition, demonstrating Taiwan’s innovation and research and development capabilities at the Taiwan Pavilion, the ministry said in a statement.

The Taiwan Pavilion showcased Taiwan’s comprehensive automotive parts supply chain and industrial strength through immersive concept cars and smart maintenance scenarios. It featured a “Digital Zone,” business meeting and product display areas, and product launches aimed at connecting Taiwanese businesses with international buyers, the ministry said.

The five-day exhibition attracted 1,970 potential buyers and visitors to the Taiwan Pavilion and generated deals worth US$147 million, it said.

In addition, the Taiwan Pavilion invited Aumovio, a German autonomous driving systems supplier, and the European Association of Automotive Suppliers to hold a session on industry trends, discussing developments in the automotive industry and green solutions in response to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, the ministry said.

The Taiwan Pavilion promoted Taiwanese products through short videos produced by influencers and held a “Taiwan Night” on the exhibition’s opening day, where 350 international buyers and representatives of automotive industry associations met with Taiwanese firms to exchange ideas and discuss cross-border cooperation, it said.

The EU is the second-largest buyer of Taiwan-made auto parts and accessories, ministry data showed.

The ministry said that with the global auto industry accelerating its digital transformation and the European market emphasizing high-quality, innovative and sustainable products, Taiwan should cooperate with Europe on auto component and automotive electronics development as well as aftermarket services.

The ministry said that the government would allocate funds to send trade delegations to international shows, while inviting potential foreign buyers here to meet Taiwanese suppliers, strike deals and expand their reach overseas.

data.title: Flash memory prices expected to climb further soon
data.description:
Prices of high-capacity NOR flash memory chips are projected to increase 90 to 110 percent in the second half of this year amid growing demand and slower capacity expansion, after jumping 100 to 120 percent on average in the first half, TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) said yesterday.

“Emerging applications such as AI servers and aerospace communications are propelling demand in 2026, aside from existing applications such as advanced driver assistance, digital cockpit systems and industrial devices,” the Taipei-based research group said in a report.

Demand from AI servers is exceptionally strong as each AI server requires three to five times more NOR flash memory capacity of a general-purpose server, TrendForce said. Edge-AI devices such as computers and robots with AI features are fueling demand for high-density NOR flash memory chips, it said.

“As NOR flash memory makers’ capacity expansions remain scant, demand-supply mismatch will carry into the second half of 2026,” TrendForce said. “NOR flash memory chip prices continue to hover at high levels, with high-capacity 256-megabit chips likely to double.”

While major memory makers have dramatically raised capital expenditures, it takes time to translate new capacity into available supply because of challenges in process shrinking, yield ramp-up, product validation and customer design-in, TrendForce said. The supply gap in the mid-to-high- capacity segment would remain unmet in the short term, it said.

However, prices of 128-megabit NOR flash memory and low-to-mid-capacity chips should see much milder increases of 10 to 20 percent in the fourth quarter, as capacity from Chinese suppliers comes online, it added.

TrendForce said Hsinchu-based Winbond Electronics Corp (華邦電), the world’s largest NOR flash memory supplier, outgrew its rivals in capacity expansion, thanks to the production ramp-up of its 45-nanometer technology and efforts to upgrade to 25 and 20-nanometer technologies.

China’s GigaDevices Semiconductor Inc (兆易創新), the second-largest NOR flash memory maker, is optimizing its product portfolio to those with capacity higher than 32 megabit, TrendForce said. The company would not see a capacity pickup until its production outsourcing efforts bear fruit in the second half of this year, it said.

Macronix International Co (旺宏), also based in Hsinchu, would see very limited capacity growth in NOR flash memory as it is strategically pivoting its 12-inch capacity to favor embedded MultiMediaCard (eMMC) products and NAND flash, a segment that is experiencing far more severe supply constraints, the researcher said.

data.title: Average wages climbing, but median wages low
data.description:
The average monthly regular wage in July was NT$49,491, a 3.32 percent increase from a year earlier and up 0.3 percent from the month before, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.

Including overtime, bonuses and other commissions, the overall monthly wage averaged NT$71,165, an annual increase of 8.25 percent and a monthly growth of 17.86 percent, the DGBAS said in a report.

In July, the median monthly wage — generally considered a more accurate measure of people’s income as extremely high or low wages do not skew it — increased 3.47 percent year-on-year and 0.3 percent month-on-month to NT$39,629, indicating that most workers still earned less than the average, the report said.

The wage data were based on the agency’s survey of employees in the nation’s industrial and service sectors. The total number of employees, including full-time and part-time employees from Taiwan or abroad, as of July 31 was 8.627 million, up 87,000 or 1.01 percent from a year earlier, the DGBAS said.

From January to July, the average monthly regular wage was NT$49,054, up 2.94 percent from the same period last year, and the median monthly wage was NT$39,341, up 3.06 percent, the report said.

After adjusting for inflation, which increased 1.8 percent annually in the first seven months, the average monthly regular wage was NT$44,113, up 1.12 percent from a year earlier and the largest increase for the same period in six years, while the median figure was NT$35,379, up 1.24 percent, it showed.

In the first seven months, cumulative total earnings (including overtime, bonuses and other non-regular earnings) grew 4.18 percent to NT$483,077 on average in the first seven months, the report said. After adjusting for inflation, the figure grew 2.33 percent, the biggest growth in 11 years, to NT$434,420, it said.

Regarding overtime hours, a key indicator of economic activity, the manufacturing sector averaged 18 hours of overtime in July, an increase of 1 hour year-on-year and reaching a nearly 16-year high for the same month, the report said.

The electronic components industry averaged 28.7 hours of overtime in July, an increase of 0.8 hours year-on-year and the highest for the same month in 47 years, while the average overtime hours in the computer, electronic products and optical products industry reached 17.1 hours, an increase of 1.3 hours year-on-year and a 43-year high for the same month, it said.

DGBAS Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said that data on the number of employees, regular wage, total wage and overtime hours all showed the overall labor market is moving in a generally positive direction.

However, with consumer inflation ticking up in the past few months and exceeding 2 percent, it could squeeze future real wage growth, she said.

data.title: BIS says global market AI momentum showing signs of vulnerability
data.description:
The artificial intelligence (AI)-linked rally that has seen world stock markets soar over the last two years is showing growing signs of vulnerability, global central bank umbrella body, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), said yesterday.

Investors were becoming "increasingly cautious" about the profitability of future AI investments, especially as the leverage of major US tech firms continued to rise, the BIS said in a report.

"The AI momentum, which had propelled equity markets and contributed to the resilience of the global economy of the last year, has begun to show growing signs of vulnerability," BIS economic analysis head Frank Smets told reporters on Friday ahead of the report’s publication.

AI-connected stocks were down sharply yesterday after the heads of a number of top AI firms warned at the weekend that the pace of the technology’s development needed to be slowed to prevent threats to humanity.

The BIS report also pointed to an uncertain global backdrop of strains on public finances, exacerbated by geopolitical tensions and volatile energy prices.

The hundreds of billions of dollars worth of debt AI firms have been issuing could also be contributing to the rise in government bond market borrowing costs, known as yields, on top of the long-held concerns about the sustainability of debt levels.

"It’s related to the fiscal fragility that comes also with higher uncertainty in the world economy," Smets said referring to the recent pressures in bond markets.

Nevertheless, he added that there were "no signs of stress" overall and that investors’ risk appetite had remained "remarkably resilient" in recent months.

Dubbed the central bank to the world’s central banks, the BIS has given regular warnings about both global debt levels and potential stock market bubbles in recent years.

"Whether this resilience (in markets) can be sustained, especially if upward pressures on yields continue, remains, however, uncertain," Smets said.

He also echoed BIS chief Pablo Hernandez de Cos’ warning last week of the financial stability risks posed by AI.

"What we are most concerned on in this (AI) area is the rapid increase in debt and leverage," Smets said. "And the fact that many of these financing deals are quite opaque. They’re often off balance sheet. They have sort of circularity in them."

The report also looked in depth at the private market funding that has been pouring into AI in recent years.

Aggregate borrowing by tech firms has risen from around US$22 billion, or 22 percent of total private credit, in 2010 to over US$1 trillion, or 44 percent, by last year. In total, outstanding loans of any type amount to almost US$2.5 trillion, it added.

Another of its studies used AI to analyse thousands of central bank speeches and reports. It showed that "core inflation" metrics that strip out energy price peaks and troughs are being cited more frequently and in greater variety.

While the trend reflected changing economic conditions, it said "the growing complexity of central bank messaging may pose challenges for effective communication with the public."

data.title: Mollusk megadeath
data.description: A man walks between wooden stakes full of mussels in a shellfish breeding farm off the coast of Bricqueville-sur-Mer, France, on Sunday. French mussel farms have been hit hard by the heat waves, and the drought has deprived them of nutrients. French mussel production has fallen by a quarter this summer, according to industry experts, who are facing an uncertain future.

data.title: KGI’s Tutoring Legacy Scholarship Marks 20 Years
data.description:
Guided by the belief that investing in education shapes the future, the China Development Foundation (CDF) is celebrating the 20th anniversary of its flagship "Tutoring Legacy Scholarship" program. Under the leadership of CDF Chairman Angelo J.Y. Koo, the initiative has spent two decades expanding horizons and creating opportunities for underserved youth across Taiwan. To date, the foundation has injected nearly NT$100 million into the program. This sustained financial commitment has empowered more than 1,500 low-income university students, who in turn have provided crucial academic guidance and mentorship to over 1,500 disadvantaged children.

By supporting university students through their studies and encouraging them to participate in after-school tutoring, the initiative accompanies underprivileged children in building academic confidence. This single resource simultaneously empowers two generations and transforms the future of two families.

Chairman Koo emphasizes that education is key to social mobility. Because financial pressure often forces bright students to prioritize survival over studies, Koo created this program to lift their economic burdens. Beyond financial aid, the initiative is designed to inspire empathy, leadership, and a lifelong dedication to giving back.

Over the past 20 years, the program has inspired countless life-changing transformations. Among them is Chen, a four-time scholarship recipient. During college, Chen became a lifeline for a vulnerable junior high student from a single-parent family who was on the verge of dropping out. Beyond patient tutoring, Chen helped the boy secure financial aid and map out a path to culinary school. A decade later, that struggling youth has become a professional chef with a thriving career and a bright, confident future.

Reflecting on this journey, Chen expressed heartfelt gratitude, stating, "The Scholarship not only alleviated my financial burden but also taught me how to listen, understand, and accompany others. Because I once received help from the foundation, I now have the opportunity to give back to society."

What began as a financial aid program has evolved over two decades into a powerful educational platform connecting youth, campuses, and communities. By fostering a "generation-mentoring-generation" model, it does not just fund dreams—it sparks a lifelong cycle of opportunity. Looking ahead, the China Development Foundation will continue to empower young leaders to join this mission, ensuring that every child has the chance to rewrite their trajectory and that this torch of hope continues to illuminate the futures of generations to come.

data.title: Central bank pressured to raise rates
data.description:
SOME CUSHION: Taiwan’s GDP is forecast to grow more than 11 percent this year, so the economy should be able to absorb the impact of a rate hike, an expert said

With domestic inflation topping the 2 percent alert level for a fourth consecutive month last month and several major central banks around the world raising their key interest rates, Taiwan’s central bank is facing growing pressure to raise rates at its quarterly policymaking meeting on Thursday, economists said.

At its June meeting, the central bank left interest rates unchanged for the ninth consecutive quarter, with the discount rate at 2 percent.

Central Bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) had said that the bank maintained a somewhat hawkish stance, with two board directors voicing support for a rate hike at the meeting.

Cathay United Bank Co (國泰世華銀行) chief economist Lin Chi-chao (林啟超) last week said that the central bank had forecast in June that the consumer price index (CPI) would rise by less than 2 percent this year.

However, the situation has since changed, as international crude oil prices have risen amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, he said.

“Inflationary pressure has been on the rise,” Lin said, citing a forecast by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics last month that CPI would increase 2.07 percent this year.

The central bank must also take into account the monetary policy moves of other major central banks when deciding whether to adjust interest rates, he said.

The Bank of Korea hiked its benchmark interest rates for a second consecutive time last month to 3 percent, Lin said.

The European Central Bank raised its key interest rates by 25 basis points last week, marking its second rate hike this year, he said, adding that there was a high possibility that the Bank of Japan would raise rates this week.

More importantly, the US Federal Reserve could raise rates this week, with the odds rising to nearly 90 percent after last month’s CPI data showed persistent inflationary pressure, Lin said.

“Whether considering domestic conditions or the international situation, the interest rate hike checklist has been fully checked,” Lin added.

With GDP growth forecast to top 11 percent this year, the economy is expected to be able to absorb the impact of a rate hike, Lin said.

Taiwan Institute of Economic Research Economic Forecasting Center director Gordon Sun (孫明德) said he expects the Fed to raise rates this week, which could serve as an indication for Taiwan’s central bank to follow suit.

If Taiwan’s rates remain unchanged, there would be a wider interest rate spread between Taiwan and the US, which is an important factor to consider, Sun said.

A central bank rate hike would not primarily be aimed at curbing inflation, but at addressing tightening liquidity in the local market, Sun added.

Fund demand has increased as companies step up investments amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, while high-flying stocks have boosted demand for funds, further tightening liquidity, he said.

Tight liquidity has pushed up market interest rates, so the central bank needs to respond by raising its key interest rates, he added.

However, Sun also raised concerns about a rate hike, saying Taiwan’s strong economic growth is largely driven by AI development, while the traditional economy has lagged behind, so higher interest rates could place a heavier financial burden on traditional industries.

data.title: Interview: NexCOBOT expects strong growth in AI controllers
data.description:
NexCOBOT Co (創博) expects robust growth in its artificial intelligence (AI) controller business this year and next year, as partnerships across a range of robotics applications begin to bear fruit, chairman Clement Lin (林茂昌) said in an interview with the Taipei Times on Monday last week.

NexCOBOT is a robotics subsidiary of industrial PC maker Nexcom International Co (新漢), where Lin also serves as chairman.

AI controller shipments are expected to exceed 1,000 units and account for about 20 percent of NexCOBOT’s controller sales next year, as the company has received orders for AI controllers for wheeled robots with humanoid upper bodies, he said, adding that the company plans to ship hundreds of units from the second half of this year through early next year.

Controller sales — including those for computer numerical control equipment, industrial robotic arms, collaborative robots and AI robotics — are expected to account for more than 20 percent of NexCOBOT’s total revenue next year, he said.

The company’s AI controllers made with higher-end Nvidia Corp computing modules could cost US$5,000 to US$8,000 per unit, significantly higher than standard controllers, which are priced at about US$1,000 each, Lin said.

NexCOBOT expects to ship about 500 advanced AI controllers based on Nvidia’s IGX Thor platform next year, up from several hundred units this year, he said.

Quadruped robot dogs and wheeled robots with humanoid upper bodies are likely to begin volume production earlier than fully bipedal humanoid robots, Lin said.

Nexcom, the Industrial Technology Research Institute and Compal Electronics Inc (仁寶) demonstrated a robot dog solution in July, drawing the interest of firefighting agencies, while wheeled robots are generally more practical than bipedal humanoids in factories, he said.

Fully bipedal humanoid robots still require major advances in vision-language-action models and multimodal AI, Lin said, adding that meaningful progress was unlikely for at least another three years.

To address the complexity of humanoid robots’ more than 20 joints, as well as the demands that heat dissipation, wiring and real-time synchronization place on AI controllers, NexCOBOT earlier this year introduced a “four-in-one” AI control platform that combines motion control, functional safety, AI computing and cybersecurity, Lin said.

With the four-in-one platform, NexCOBOT adds its own I/O baseboards, communications, and control hardware and software to computing modules from Nvidia and Intel Corp, enabling components such as joints, vision modules, dexterous hands, thermal-imaging systems and predictive maintenance tools to be directly integrated and operated together, he said.

“While industrial PC suppliers typically provide only graphics cards or hardware baseboards, NexCOBOT aims to offer a more complete ‘last-mile’ solution to help system makers develop and deploy robots faster,” Lin said.

Last month, NexCOBOT unveiled its “RoboWIZ AI Robot Open Platform” to bring together dozens of robotics ecosystem partners and support the development of humanoid, quadruped and dual-arm robots, while allowing customers to focus on robot design, dynamic balancing, application development and commercialization, thereby shrinking the time to market, Lin said.

Taiwanese robotics partners mainly supply cameras, thermal-imaging and predictive maintenance technologies, while functional safety joints, complete 3D vision modules and advanced dexterous hands still require the support of European and US partners, he said.

NexCOBOT works with motion control supplier Synapticon GmbH on developing functional safety joints, he added.

Nexcom plans to establish RoboWiz hubs in Taipei, Taichung and at the Curiosity Lab in Atlanta, Georgia, to serve robot system makers and engage with local ecosystem partners, Lin said.

The company also aims to leverage Taiwan’s information and communications technology integration capabilities to expand AI robotics supply chain cooperation and position the country as a key partner for US robotics development and non-China supply chains, he said.
